title: Why Your House Gets Dusty So Fast Out Here
metaTitle: Why Your House Gets Dusty So Fast in the Desert | Las Cruces
metaDescription: Mesilla Valley houses take on more dust than most. Cut the supply first with mats and filters, then clean high to low, damp not dry, floors last.
summary: The supply of dust here is genuinely higher, so the first move is cutting it off, not cleaning harder.
transcript: A house in the Mesilla Valley gets dusty faster than the same house almost anywhere east of here, and it isn't because you're cleaning wrong.
The supply is different. Open desert, thin vegetation, and spring wind that runs for days at a time. The particles are fine and mineral, and they stay airborne long enough to find any opening.

The buildings are different too. Swamp coolers pull outside air in all summer. Windows get opened through the shoulder seasons. And most houses here have some mix of tile, stucco and screen doors, none of which seal the way a closed-up, refrigerated-air house does.
So the first move isn't cleaning harder. It's cutting the supply.

Doormats, inside and out, at every door people actually use. Most of what ends up on your floors walked in on someone's shoes. A coarse mat outside to knock it loose and a mat inside to catch the rest does more than any product you can buy.
Change HVAC filters more often than the box says. That interval assumes an average dust load and this isn't one. If a filter looks loaded at a month, replace it at a month.
Check the weatherstripping on exterior doors. If you can see daylight under a door, that gap is running wide open through every wind event.
Then the cleaning, in the order that works. Dust before you vacuum, vacuum before you mop. Each one of those puts material down onto the next surface, so out of order means doing it twice.

Damp, not dry. A dry cloth or a feather duster relocates fine dust into the air, where it settles again over the next few hours, which is exactly why a room you cleaned yesterday looks dusty this morning. A barely damp microfiber traps it instead.
High to low in every room. Fan blades, then shelves and frames, then furniture, then floors.

Soft surfaces are the reservoir. Curtains, upholstery, rugs and bedding hold far more than hard surfaces and let it go slowly every time someone sits down or a fan comes on. If the house feels dusty a day after a full clean, that's where it's coming from, and it's the part that never gets done.

One note on vacuums. You want a sealed path, not just a HEPA label on the filter. A machine that leaks around the filter housing blows the finest particles, the ones that hang in the air longest, straight back into the room.
localNote: Spring is the hard season. Wind events through March and April can undo a full clean in an afternoon, and no cleaning strategy beats a day of blowing dust. The practical answer is to shut the house during the event and clean once it's passed, not while it's running.

faq.q: Am I doing something wrong if the dust is back in two days?
faq.a: Probably not. The supply here is genuinely higher than most places. Check the soft surfaces and the filters before you change how you clean.
For airborne particles in one room, yes. They do nothing about what's already settled into carpet and upholstery.

faq.q: Is a feather duster ever fine?
faq.a: On something you dust weekly, sure. On real accumulation it just puts it back into the air.
Mats at the doors. It's unglamorous and it beats everything else.
